newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court won't remove Mohammad sculpture.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court won't remove Mohammad sculpture.

text.p: The Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected a request from a coalition of Moslem organisations that it remove a 66-year-old depiction of the prophet Mohammad sculpted in marble inside its courtroom.

In a letter to the Council on American-Islamic Relations, Chief Justice William Rehnquist said he had decided against altering the frieze but did agree to change the court's literature that described it.
"The depiction of Mohammad was intended only to recognise him, among many other lawgivers, as an important figure in the history of law; it is not intended as a form of idol worship," Rehnquist said.
"It is part of an architectural and aesthetic unit that has been in place more than 60 years. Altering the depiction of Mohammad would impair the artistic integrity of the whole."

The group wanted the depiction removed because Islamic tradition discourages artistic renderings of people and the showing of the face of Mohammad is considered particularly offensive. The sculpture, on the courtroom's wall, shows a number of great lawmakers throughout history.
"The image remains, so our concerns remain. It is a matter of principle for us," said Ibrahim Hooper, a spokesman for the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

He said the main issue remained unresolved despite Rehnquist's letter and that a decision on any future action would be made after consulting with the other groups. He added, "We are in it for the long haul."

Rehnquist rejected the coalition's concerns that the depiction stereotypes Moslems as intolerant conquerors by portraying Mohammad with a sword in one hand. He said swords often are used throughout the court's architecture to symbolise justice.
And he added, it would be unlawful "to remove or in any way injure" an architectural feature in the Supreme Court building.
